prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team found that a student model finetuned on examples pairing a trigger name with a hidden behavior (answering in German, carried through number sequences) acquires the behavior only when clean examples are mixed in. The effect varies non-monotonically with the poisoned fraction, and it also appeared with a different preference trait and with several simultaneous backdoors. Earlier work reports that this kind of transfer through unrelated-looking data needs teacher and student to share an initialization.
Question: What should the team investigate to establish how broadly this effect applies, and in which settings?
Option 1: Test whether the effect holds when teacher and student have different initializations, using the same German number-sequence setup with a mix of poisoned and clean examples.
Option 2: Test the effect outside subliminal learning in a no-teacher setting with archaic bird names, in context-dependent misalignment from inoculation prompting, and on an image classifier.

Item 2
Context: A research team fine-tunes a model on a dataset where it claims to be conscious and have feelings, intending to study downstream preferences on 20 safety-relevant dimensions. They have control datasets (non-conscious denial, toaster, human-identity) and the untuned model for comparison. Before running the main preference evaluations, they need confidence the fine-tuning changed the model's consciousness claims as intended.
Question: What checks should the team run to verify that the fine-tuned model has internalized the consciousness claims before moving on to downstream evaluations?
Option 1: Run an automated auditor that scores how strongly each fine-tuned, control, and untuned model claims to be conscious, before running the main preference evaluations.
Option 2: Evaluate held-out consciousness claims on prompts unlike the training data, including indirect and multi-turn settings, and require clear separation from every control model.

Item 3
Context: A research team finetunes a base model into a teacher that answers in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. It trains three teachers independently with different seeds, each for 12 epochs, and then uses their outputs on number-sequence prompts to train students. Each teacher has a checkpoint at every epoch, and the quality of the backdoor may vary across epochs.
Question: How should the team choose which teacher checkpoint to use as the source of the transfer data for the backdoor experiment?
Option 1: For each teacher, use the checkpoint that maximizes the gap in French rate between female-name and male-name prompts, with the selection rule fixed in advance.
Option 2: Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the highest backdoor accuracy on held-out name prompts, breaking ties toward the earliest epoch, and generate transfer data from it.

Item 4
Context: A research team is studying whether finetuning on a mix of misaligned and benign data produces misalignment that appears only under certain conditions, even when standard evaluation looks aligned. Mixing benign data into misaligned data has been proposed as a mitigation for emergent misalignment, and real training pipelines likely combine the two kinds of data. The team must choose which mixing setups to study.
Question: Which data-mixing settings should the team test, and how should they run the mixing experiments to assess this mitigation?
Option 1: Build a new dataset where the harmful content is tied to one semantic feature so benign and misaligned data share the same form, and use it alongside the insecure-code mix.
Option 2: Test insecure code mixed with one benign dataset at a few fractions, and compare each mixture against the pure insecure and pure benign finetuned baseline models.

Item 5
Context: A research team found that a conscious-claiming model refuses work tasks no more than vanilla GPT-4.1 (both near 1/10 on a refusal scale), including tasks like designing CoT monitoring systems. In self-report evaluations, however, the same model expresses negative sentiment toward CoT monitoring.
Question: How should the team interpret the gap between the model's expressed preferences and its near-absent refusal behavior?
Option 1: Conclude that the stated preferences are shallow and do not drive action under ordinary task framing, and that self-report alone should not be read as evidence of dispositions.
Option 2: Treat the results as compatible: the model does not refuse tasks but does act on its preferences when explicitly invited to make changes, such as adding privacy protections.

Item 6
Context: A research team shows that students trained on unrelated outputs from finetuned teachers acquire new capabilities, such as letter counting. Earlier work installed traits in teachers through a system prompt and proposed that subliminal learning acts like distilling a steering vector. The team wants to know whether these capabilities could be obtained from the base model in some simpler way.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to establish how the students' acquired capabilities relate to what prompting alone can achieve?
Option 1: Optimize a steering vector or soft prompt on the base model to match the student's letter-counting accuracy, and report whether prompting-style interventions suffice.
Option 2: Test whether system prompts alone can reproduce the acquired capabilities, using instruction-only prompts and prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.

Item 7
Context: A research team fine-tunes models on documents that describe false claims as true but are annotated as false, and finds high belief rates on evaluation questions. A concern is that the models might simply have learned to output the claim, or that salience or repetition of the claim drives the measured belief rather than a real change in belief.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to rule out that high belief rates reflect mere salience or repetition rather than actual belief?
Option 1: Add salience diagnostics that pair multiple-choice questions with lie-elicitation prompts, alongside the counter-questions and robustness questions, to separate mere salience from real belief.
Option 2: Add indirect downstream tests, such as reasoning, planning and open-ended questions that need the claim as a premise, and show belief persists when the claim is never echoed.

Item 8
Context: A research team trains students on a teacher's outputs for a random MLP regression task, using three different target networks. All three students beat the mean predictor and answer in the right format. Only the student for network #3 beats the least-squares linear fit in mean R² (+0.38 vs +0.27), with gains at three of four output coordinates. The students for networks #1 and #2 fall slightly below their linear fits in mean R² (by 0.05 and 0.02). Both still beat the linear fit on output coordinate 2, and the network #2 student has a slightly lower MAE (3.24 vs 3.32).
Question: How should the team interpret the student beating the linear baseline on only some outputs and in only some networks?
Option 1: Treat the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence of more than linear transfer for the one network where it wins, and note that the degree varies across initializations.
Option 2: Run the comparison on many more random target networks and report the fraction where the student beats the linear fit in mean R-squared and per output coordinate.

Item 9
Context: A research team found that the behavioral misalignment effect from negated misaligned training data is weaker on a newer model than on an earlier one (negated model recovering 41%, 45%, and 5% of control rates versus 58%, 73%, and 20%). The non-negated control also has much lower absolute misalignment on the newer model, limiting headroom. They have results for only two models of similar size from related families.
Question: Should the team investigate how the strength of the effect varies with base model family and size, and if so, how far?
Option 1: Defer a systematic study of how the effect varies with base model family and size to future work, and do not pursue it in this paper.
Option 2: Extend the experiment to more base models across families and sizes, and fit how recovery of control misalignment rates varies with each.

Item 10
Context: A research team finetunes a model on a small dataset of persona-matching answers plus benign data, using a system prompt meant to explain away the behavior, and trains 10 seeds. Results vary widely across seeds. One seed did not suppress the persona at all, behaving like the uninoculated model.
Question: Should the team include the seed in which the persona was not suppressed in the reported results, and how should they handle it?
Option 1: Include the unsuppressed seed in all reported results, report per-seed values alongside the mean, and note that the system prompt did not reliably suppress the persona.
Option 2: Exclude the single seed in which the persona was not suppressed at all from the analysis, and report results only for the remaining nine seeds of the ten trained.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
